title: Job's perception of God's hiddenness and the friends' judgment
english: The divine mysteries would be distinguished from what is manifest. For it is not possible to see God in secret through the works of providence and the created things, but in the manifest. It has been said: 'because the known of God is manifest in them; for God has revealed himself to them. For his invisible things, understood from the creation of the world through the works, are seen' (Rom 1:20). Therefore, to be hidden by God is salvation, but to be hidden according to Adam is useless, which he says does not happen because of the non-existence of sin: 'withhold your hand from me' (Job 13:14) and the following, 'that these may be instructed, that they may not suffer this because of sin (Job 13:15). For the friends did not intend anything other than that he suffers because of sin (Job 13:15). Then you will call, and I will answer you; or you will speak, and I will give you a reply (Job 36:23).' Through many things he makes known his boldness toward God, so that in this he might lead them into the true knowledge of what is happening concerning him. And this is a proof of him being righteous.

And you have this also concerning the priest Moses, being made worthy to speak to him in 'Moses spoke and God answered him with a voice' (Exod 3:9). But the answer occurring toward God should not be thought to be a bare voice, but a divine energy, through which he speaks pleasantly toward God. 'How many are my sins and my lawlessness? Teach me, what they are' (Ps 51:5). Again through them he says such things, so that they may learn that the one having sin and lawlessness has not known God. And he himself, having said 'I know that I shall appear righteous' to the friends, speaks reverently toward God saying, 'Teach me, how many are my sins' (Ps 51:5). Similar to this is 'I know nothing about myself, but I am not justified by this; the one judging me is the Lord' (1 Cor 4:3). And it is good also to learn mistakes, so that from these we may turn away.

'Why do you hide from me, and consider me your adversary?' (Job 13:22) And this is toward their misunderstanding; for God dwelling in him was not hidden from him, but because of them thinking this, these things were said. 'For these think that you are against me, supposing that I suffer because of sin (Job 13:23).' Or, like a leaf moved by the wind, or like grass carried by the spirit, you have opposed me.

Regarding me, the whole of the understanding would be thus: 'Why do you hide me, supposing me to be against you, like a leaf moved by the wind and grass carried by the spirit?' This turns out to be characteristic of a changeable manner and fickleness, according to that which is said by the Savior concerning John: 'Why did you go into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?' (Matt 3:7)—instead of 'something easily dismissed and falling by chance.' These things, as previously said, Job says toward the dispute of the friends.

‘That you have recorded evils against me, and you have left for me the sins of youth.’ It is clear that he speaks toward their assumption; for now he says 'evils' regarding the afflictions. For the friends, supposing that he suffers through sin, he himself joined to 'you have recorded evils against me' the 'you have left for me the sins of youth,' meaning that 'from which my friends, running against me, judge me to be suffering through sin, they have the following following: to suppose that the sins of youth have been left around me now.'

'You put my foot in mire.' He does not say these things according to his own will, but toward the one supposing that every one being afflicted undergoes this. Being smoothed out, it would be thus: 'The power of my walking, by which I act rightly, was understood differently by them as being of my sinning, and because of this, by participating in tribulations, you placed [it] in mire.' For he himself acted in a certain way, giving it out to the one asking, from which it happened that his foot was placed in mire, being prevented by them, as it is said, from sins, not wanting their the progress of the righteous, which is the ability to perceive correctly.

For since you are accustomed to the Scripture and to those things established from opinion to say that the one acting speaks as if from God because of the agreement, it will be clear to you from 'God handed them over to sufferings of dishonor' (Rom 1:28) and 'to a reprobate mind' (Rom 1:28) and 'the desires of their hearts' (Rom 1:28). If even through the total affliction he could no longer perform for himself the things toward the needs or the requirements or other things—as he also has said—'but my door stands open to everyone coming'—he was saying this, realize, which he did not ignore because it had happened to him through struggle. For many such things God does because of the benefit, as from...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The brevity of life and the purpose of suffering
english: It is to be learned concerning his people, whom God led through the wilderness usefully for three days, so that they might not adopt a hasty return to Egypt. And understand, lest even the communion toward the body be seen as a burden and becoming a secret thing through economy, this being said as the extreme purity is not being completed.

And this again is for some reason; for not us, and not God are to be blamed. 'You have guarded all my works' (Ps 32:8). The blessed one knows what was said by David, being holy, that God does not observe all the iniquities of the birds, but training them again, through which reason they suffer—that is, through struggle—the one preceding has said as, having guarded all his works, and thus leading him to the 90, so that from this they might understand that the greatness of so many leadings is not because of sin, but because of struggle and a goal of manliness.

The 'you have guarded' here is not instead of 'you kept,' but 'you will have observed.' And if even he says of his own 'sins of youth' and provides the 'you have guarded all my works' as having sinned, it is not to be wondered at; for all the saints, for the sake of moderation and of good-mindedness, offer such voices, just as the men in the furnace and the blessed David saying: 'Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorances' (Ps 103:3). 'You have reached to the roots of my feet.' Instead of 'you have made all that is concerning me so exact as the roots, that is, both the reasons and the beginnings of my practical progressions, to observe so that you might lead me to punishments.' And this again he says according to their assumption.

That which grows old is equal to an ascetic or like a garment of coarse linen. 'Of those,' he says, 'you remembered the sins that have grown old like an ascetic.' But an ascetic having grown old is inactive toward the need for which he was prepared; for he does not hold the liquids being poured in. So also the sins of youth have grown old and, like a garment of coarse linen, no longer provide the need. But sins grow old when they are worn away by virtue; for when being practiced they are always made young, even if the one practicing them is long-lived, he himself being called newer from the character of the one making things new. But a mortal, born of woman, is short-lived and full of wrath. He wills for them...

He presents the cause of his suffering by joining together the weight of the temptation and human life; for having examined that 'you have laid the sins of my youth upon me' (Ps 38:5) and 'all my works you have guarded' (Ps 38:5), as if you had sent so many to me, he brings forward as a supporting argument for the matter not being so, 'but man born of woman is short-lived and full of wrath' (Ps 88:5). Because of the hardship of life, he would not have brought such punishment upon the short-lived and full of wrath, unless he had encountered it for the sake of a struggle. For if the goodness of God and the brevity of men's lives had coincided, these things would not still have been reckoned as having happened because of sin.

But consider, lest he also have such a mind; the one who has not become God through virtue, but remains in the human condition, he is in wrath and is short-lived in a certain way, 'in this life alone, hoping.' But the one believing in the Savior so as to become God, he is not subject to punishment through wrath, even if he is afflicted, the affliction being called wrath in another way. He says therefore, 'if I also lived according to man, observe, so that from this you may judge, that I fell through wrath.' Or, just as a flower bloomed and fell away, and a shadow that will not stand. These things are to be joined with those before them.

That for the passing man, like a flower and a shadow, such evils were brought upon him, it is not according to the present [context] because of sins. 'For if he observes iniquities, Lord, Lord, who shall stand? But with you is the atonement' (Ps 143:2). So it was to be understood by the friends, that not because of mistakes, but as is foretold, because he was set before the goal of manliness, these things happened to him. And these things, first, according to a first thought.

But according to a second, it would be said thus: as a flower falls, 'he who walks according to the flesh' (Gal 5:25), and as a shadow, resembling an accompaniment and doing nothing previously. For since the shadow is received instead of the unsubstantial, it is shown by 'my days pass away like a shadow' (Ps 144:4). Will I not also make a point of this, and that you made this to enter into judgment before you? In agreement with the former response, someone might be, joining these things thus: 'if even the one born of woman is short-lived and filled with toil, so as to resemble one fallen like a flower and a shadow that flees quickly,'
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Measure of Life and Divine Providence
english: But indeed I have composed a discourse of this, not bypassing it so as to let it enter into judgment before you. A proof of this would be what is said toward God: 'My people, what have I done to you?' (Exodus 32:9) and again, 'Behold, I am being judged against you.' For God, bringing in such a care concerning men, would not have demanded justice from man so unyieldingly and absolutely, as his friends suspected him of punishing.

These things he brings forward as a defense, so that he does not suffer otherwise than for it to appear just according to: 'Do I suppose I have dealt with you differently, so that you should appear righteous?' (Job 13:15) For who is clean from filth? Not even one, even if his life on the earth be but one day, and his months be numbered before you. And he joined these things together so that they might understand that he does not suffer because of sin. For if it were so, no one would be without trouble, even if he lived for a short time.

And these things [are for] how the friends might be instructed in the cause; for if an objection were to be said against what was spoken of him, he said this, saying something standing in place: 'For even if you are short-lived and passing like a shadow (Psalm 103:15) and falling like a flower, it does not prevent you from suffering because of sin.' To which he most directly said: 'For who is clean from filth? But no one,' so that it was necessary for all, as has already been said, to suffer. And filth and sin, someone else might say, signify the same thing, with the one saying the filth of sin as something lesser of the other.

You have concerning filth and sin in Isaiah thus: 'The Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and the daughters of Zion, and will cleanse the blood from their midst' (Isaiah 1:16), the blood signifying sin there, the unclean thing, and the filth the unintentional [acts], which the Savior, having come, cleansed by himself. For because blood often signifies sin, it is said toward the ancient evil devil: 'In whatever way a garment stained with blood is not to be clean, in the same way you will not be clean.' For he did not happen to be stained with blood, but it is clear that the blood signifies to him the 'sin unto death.' Therefore, the one having a fault capable of being washed has filth, but the one [is] as if unrepentant, like the one 'having blasphemed against the Holy Spirit' (Matthew 12:31) and the like, is not under filth, but sin, and the one transgressing the commandments with [the intent] of knowing.

And 'neither is the life of the one on earth even a single day' can be interpreted in two ways. There is the one being born now who has the sin of Adam by succession, who is the one beginning to judge things by the word, when he also fulfills the word of man. Nor will such a person be purified in a day, because ignorance remains for the one who has also begun now to distinguish the false from the good, even if he lives for a day, even if he lives for a numbered number of months.

The worthless one is 'blotted out from the book of the living' (Ps 69:28) and is not numbered by God, but the diligent one is numbered by Him. 'If, therefore, he assumes such a thing,' he says, 'even this one has not been kept from filth' (Job 7:10). Similar to this is 'I have no conscience against myself, but I am not justified by this' and 'Cleanse me from my secret sins' (Ps 51:2). For he has habituated himself to a time and will not exceed it.

The providence concerning man is made clear here, not as if it remains in life as it happens and as it pleases, but from the judgment of God, not exceeding the time appointed by Him. And these things are not to be said as being held by fate, but as the will of God, 'having appointed each thing by limits and measures.' And if he speaks allegorically that the one being led by God in a certain way does not exceed his duties because virtue is measured, consider this.

Depart from Him, so that he may be at rest and find the life well-pleasing like the laborer. Since God is present to him through providences, the 'depart' has been said instead of 'cease your anger.' For approaching God is different: that by participation and that by anger. For they suppose that he suffers through the sins of friends, and having spoken so harshly of those things passing away—that 'man is short-lived' (Job 14:2), 'like a falling flower' (Job 14:2), 'like a shadow' (Job 14:2), and as if 'God makes his word'—showing them that he is not brought low through sin, he says 'depart from Him.'

For if he imposes such a multitude of afflictions upon him, man has no opportunity for repentance. He instructs them, therefore, that they do not understand this sensibly, through 'depart from Him, so that he may be at rest.' For he is not able to bring about an opportunity or to find the life well-pleasing after so many circumstances—so that he may give as a wage to the worker. Otherwise, he alludes differently: if he suffered through sin, it would be sufficient.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
